sections.title: Cell Cycle Regulation and Its Link to Cancer

blocks.x: Every human cell is bounded and organized by membranes that create distinct compartments, each specialized for a set of biochemical tasks. A cell's shape is determined mainly by its function (a red blood cell is a biconcave disc for gas diffusion; a neuron is elongated for signal conduction; a sperm cell is streamlined for motility) — this function-first principle is a common exam point. Complete cells always contain ribosomes, but not every particle seen under the microscope is a true organelle: a microsome, for instance, is not a real structure inside the living cell — it is an artificial vesicle formed from fragmented endoplasmic reticulum when cells are homogenized in the lab, so it is correctly excluded from lists of "organelles present in a complete/intact cell."
The plasma membrane is a fluid mosaic of a phospholipid bilayer embedded with proteins, cholesterol, and glycolipids. Functionally:

items: Phospholipids form the structural bilayer and give the membrane its basic permeability barrier and fluidity.
Membrane proteins (integral and peripheral) provide channels, pumps, receptors, and enzymatic activity.

Carbohydrates (as glycoproteins and glycolipids forming the glycocalyx) are the molecules primarily responsible for cell-to-cell recognition and immune identity (e.g., ABO blood group antigens are carbohydrate structures attached to membrane glycolipids/glycoproteins).

blocks.x: The freeze-fracture technique — where a frozen membrane is cleaved and the fracture face examined by electron microscopy — is a classic method for studying the internal architecture of both the plasma membrane and the nuclear envelope, since both are lipid bilayers that split along their hydrophobic midline.

The nucleus is enclosed by a double-membraned nuclear envelope (outer and inner nuclear membranes), continuous with the rough ER. The narrow space between the outer and inner nuclear membranes is called the perinuclear space — note that "periplasm" is a distinct term properly used for the space between the inner and outer membranes of Gram-negative bacteria, not the nuclear envelope, which makes statements equating the two a classic "mismatched pairing" exam trap.

The envelope is perforated by nuclear pores (nuclear pore complexes), which regulate bidirectional traffic of RNA and proteins between nucleus and cytoplasm. Inside, the nucleolus is the site of ribosomal RNA transcription and ribosome subunit assembly. Importantly, nuclear size does not simply track chromosome number — it is determined more by the cell's metabolic/synthetic activity (nucleocytoplasmic ratio, ploidy of DNA content, and transcriptional demand) than by the count of chromosomes present.
The ER is a continuous membranous network with two functionally distinct regions:

c: Synthesis of secretory, membrane, and lysosomal proteins; forms vacuoles and protein bodies
Lipid/steroid synthesis, drug and toxin detoxification, calcium storage
Glucose-6-phosphatase (releases free glucose from glucose-6-phosphate, especially abundant in liver SER — the final step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis)

blocks.x: The ER is contiguous with the nuclear envelope and participates broadly in producing membrane-bound compartments (vacuoles, protein bodies, and in plants/fungi, structures like glyoxysomes), making it a central hub of the endomembrane system.

The Golgi is a stack of flattened, curved cisternae (cis face facing the ER, trans face facing the plasma membrane) that receives vesicles from the RER, further modifies proteins (glycosylation, sulfation, proteolytic processing), sorts them, and packages them into vesicles for secretion, membrane insertion, or delivery to lysosomes. It is central to the cell's vesicular trafficking and secretory pathway.

Lysosomes are membrane-bound vesicles from the Golgi containing acid hydrolases (proteases, nucleases, lipases, glycosidases) active at low pH, responsible for intracellular digestion, autophagy, and turnover of organelles. Uncontrolled or dysregulated autophagy is linked to carcinogenesis, and defective lysosomal enzymes underlie the lysosomal storage diseases:

items: Hurler syndrome — deficiency of a specific lysosomal enzyme (alpha-L-iduronidase), NOT absence of lysosomes themselves (a common exam distractor).
Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II) — deficiency of lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase, causing liver (and cardiac/skeletal muscle) cells to become engorged with glycogen.
Tay-Sachs disease — hexosaminidase A deficiency, ganglioside accumulation in neurons.
Fabry disease — alpha-galactosidase A deficiency; because the gene is X-linked, it manifests as a serious disease predominantly (though not with absolute exclusivity) in males.

blocks.x: Peroxisomes are single-membrane organelles containing oxidative enzymes (catalase, oxidases) that detoxify hydrogen peroxide and handle very-long-chain fatty acid beta-oxidation and bile acid/plasmalogen synthesis. They are especially concentrated in the liver and kidney for detoxification, and are notably abundant in brown fat, where they support the high oxidative metabolism linked to non-shivering thermogenesis. Peroxisomes do not contain "oxysomes" — oxysomes (F0F1 particles) are a mitochondrial/chloroplast structure, not a peroxisomal one.

Mitochondria are double-membraned, semi-autonomous organelles — the "powerhouse of the cell" — with a smooth outer membrane and a highly folded inner membrane (cristae) that greatly increases surface area for oxidative phosphorylation. Key structural/functional points:

items: The inner membrane houses the electron transport chain and the ATP synthase (F0F1 particle, also called an oxysome), which uses the proton gradient built across the inner membrane to phosphorylate ADP to ATP (chemiosmotic coupling). The inner membrane is characteristically impermeable to H+ ions except through this channel — this impermeability is essential for maintaining the proton-motive force.

The matrix contains the enzymes of the citric acid (Krebs) cycle. During the mitochondrion's actively respiring state, oxygen consumption and ATP output rise while the Krebs cycle intermediates are drawn down/turned over rapidly (a state described in some texts as the Krebs cycle being transiently "reduced" in level while flux through the ETC/oxidative phosphorylation increases).

Mitochondria possess their own small circular genome (mtDNA), and their own ribosomes and machinery for transcription/translation, reflecting their semi-autonomy. Both mitochondrial and chloroplast gene expression are notably inhibited by antibiotics that target prokaryotic-type machinery — chloramphenicol (blocks the prokaryotic-type large ribosomal subunit/translation) and rifampicin (blocks a prokaryotic-type RNA polymerase) — a direct legacy of their bacterial ancestry, whereas eukaryotic nuclear transcription/translation is instead blocked by alpha-amanitin and cycloheximide, respectively.

Mitochondria are dynamic: they can move (via cytoskeletal motors), change shape/position within the cell, and undergo fission and fusion ("changing set") — i.e., essentially all of the listed mitochondrial behaviors (movement, position change, and changing shape/number) occur.

Endosymbiotic theory, first postulated by Lynn Margulis, proposes that mitochondria (and chloroplasts) arose from free-living aerobic bacteria (and cyanobacteria, respectively) engulfed by an ancestral eukaryotic host cell, explaining their own genome, double membrane, and bacteria-like ribosomes.

Since nuclear DNA also encodes many mitochondrial/chloroplast proteins, organelle function requires cooperation between the nuclear and organellar genomes — the enzyme ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase (RuBisCO) is a textbook example: its large subunit is chloroplast-encoded while its small subunit is nuclear-encoded.

Mitochondrial (maternal) inheritance: because sperm contribute essentially no mitochondria to the zygote, genes carried on mtDNA are inherited only from the mother — this is the molecular basis of maternally inherited traits and diseases, distinguishing mtDNA inheritance from classic Mendelian nuclear inheritance.

blocks.x: Ribosomes are ribonucleoprotein particles (not membrane-bound, so technically an "organelle without a membrane") that translate mRNA into protein. They are the one organelle-type structure present across all five kingdoms of life (Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia) since all cellular life needs translation machinery — unlike the nucleus, ER, or mitochondria, which are absent from prokaryotes. Free ribosomes make cytosolic proteins; RER-bound ribosomes make secreted/membrane proteins.

c: Maintain cell shape, intracellular transport (with motor proteins), spindle fibers, form cilia/flagella and centrioles; assist (with microfilaments) in cell movement
Varies by cell type: keratin (epithelia), vimentin (mesenchymal cells), desmin (muscle), neurofilaments (neurons), lamins (nuclear lamina)

blocks.x: Because intermediate filaments are built from several different tissue-specific proteins, a question asking what they are "composed of" among keratin, vimentin, and desmin is correctly answered all of these — each is a valid intermediate filament protein in a different cell lineage.

Within microtubules, the motor protein dynein forms the cross-bridging "arms" seen in ultrastructural studies of ciliary/flagellar axonemes (the classic 9+2 arrangement) and drives minus-end-directed movement, distinguishing it from kinesin (plus-end directed) and from cytoskeletal structural proteins like desmin or vimentin.

Each centriole is a cylindrical structure built from nine triplets of microtubules (9+0 arrangement) and is chemically rich in both tubulin (structural protein) and ATPase (providing mechanical/motor-associated activity). A pair of centrioles plus surrounding pericentriolar material forms the centrosome, the main microtubule-organizing center that duplicates once per cell cycle and organizes the mitotic spindle poles. Basal bodies are structurally identical to centrioles, and it is centrioles/basal bodies from which cilia and flagella arise, templating the axoneme that grows from them.

items: Tight junctions (zonula occludens): seal adjacent epithelial cells together, blocking paracellular diffusion and maintaining apical/basal membrane polarity.
Desmosomes: spot-like anchoring junctions linking intermediate filaments (keratin in epithelia) between cells, providing mechanical strength against shearing forces.

Gap junctions: composed of connexon channels that directly connect the cytoplasm of adjacent cells, allowing passage of ions and small molecules — the structural basis of electrical and metabolic coupling between cells (e.g., cardiac myocytes, some neurons).

blocks.x: Together these junctions let tissues function as coordinated units rather than isolated cells.

sections.title: Cell Cycle Regulation and Its Link to Cancer

blocks.x: Although the phase-by-phase mechanics of the cell cycle are covered elsewhere, the key regulatory proteins are core "cell biology" content because their loss or dysregulation is central to carcinogenesis:

items: p53 ("guardian of the genome"): a tumor suppressor activated by DNA damage; it halts the cycle (commonly at the G1/S checkpoint) to allow repair, or triggers apoptosis if damage is irreparable. Loss-of-function mutations in TP53 are the single most common genetic alteration across human cancers.

Retinoblastoma protein (pRb): another key tumor suppressor; in its hypophosphorylated (active) state it binds and inhibits the E2F transcription factor, blocking progression into S phase. Cyclin-CDK–mediated phosphorylation of pRb releases E2F and permits the G1/S transition. Loss of RB function (as in retinoblastoma and many other cancers) removes this brake.

Cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs): cyclin levels rise and fall through the cycle, activating specific CDK partners at the right time (e.g., cyclin D-CDK4/6 and cyclin E-CDK2 drive the G1/S transition; cyclin B-CDK1 drives entry into mitosis). This system is a major target of dysregulation in cancer (e.g., cyclin D or CDK4 amplification).

Checkpoints: surveillance mechanisms (G1/S, G2/M, and the spindle-assembly/metaphase checkpoint) that halt the cycle if DNA damage, incomplete replication, or misaligned chromosomes are detected — ensuring damaged or incompletely-processed cells don't proceed to division.

Oncogenes vs. tumor suppressor genes: oncogenes are activated/gain-of-function forms of normal proto-oncogenes that drive proliferation when overactive (e.g., RAS, MYC); tumor suppressor genes (like TP53, RB1, and NF1) normally restrain proliferation or promote apoptosis/repair, and cancer typically requires their loss-of-function (often on both alleles).

Neurofibromatosis (due to loss of the NF1 tumor suppressor gene) is a classic clinical correlate, presenting with pigmented skin lesions (café-au-lait spots) alongside neurofibromas — an example of a tumor suppressor gene disorder with a recognizable cutaneous sign.

Cells that permanently exit the active cycle enter a quiescent resting state (G0). Being in G0 does not mean a cell is destined to die, nor does it mean the cell has duplicated (4n) DNA — G0 cells retain the normal diploid (2n) DNA content of G1, simply paused outside the cycle. Fully differentiated, non-dividing postmitotic cells such as neurons (and, essentially, skeletal/cardiac muscle cells) are the classic example of permanent G0 arrest in adult humans, in contrast to actively renewing tissues like liver (which retains regenerative capacity) or kidney and skin. Cells growing in laboratory culture can also enter and exit G0, so it is incorrect to say cultured cells can never be found in this state.
